objectives: Explain why a port scan is easy to spot on an industrial network
Describe how a threshold rule with a time window detects a scan
Find and read a port_scan alert on the CybICS IDS dashboard and API
Identify ways a scan can stay below a threshold rule
takeaways: A port scan is one source trying many ports in a short time, which normal clients never do.
The CybICS port_scan rule alerts when one source tries 5 or more ports on one target within 10 seconds.
The IDS dashboard on port 8443 and its API show alerts and per-rule counts.
Every threshold has an edge: slow, wide or non-SYN scans can slip under this one.
Detection only helps if someone reads the alerts; a firewall reduces what a scan can find.

checkpoints.question: Your scanner probes 4 ports on the PLC within 3 seconds. Does the CybICS port_scan rule fire?
options: Yes, 4 ports in 3 seconds is fast enough
No, it needs 5 different ports in 10 s
Only if one of the probed ports is open
checkpoints.explanation: The rule needs at least 5 distinct destination ports from one source to one target inside its 10-second window; speed alone does not count. Whether the ports are open does not matter either; the rule counts connection attempts.

quiz.question: Why is a port scan easier to detect on an industrial network than on an office network?
options: Plant traffic is predictable, so new ports stand out
Industrial protocols log every connection attempt
Industrial switches block and report scans by default
Plant networks have fewer hosts for a scan to hide in
quiz.explanation: In a plant the same devices talk to the same ports all day, so a host touching many new ports is unusual. Industrial protocols and switches do not log or block scans on their own; on an office network many users open many connections, so unusual behaviour hides more easily.

quiz.question: An attacker checks port 502 on 30 different hosts within 5 seconds. Does the CybICS port_scan rule fire?
options: Yes, 30 attempts is far above the threshold
No, each target sees only one port
Yes, because port 502 is a Modbus port
No, port 502 is a normal plant service
quiz.explanation: The rule groups by source and target. A wide scan of one port touches each target once, so no pair reaches 5 ports, even though the total of 30 attempts sounds like a lot. Counting per source across all targets would catch it.

quiz.question: You scan twice within 20 seconds. How many port_scan alerts from your address should you expect?
options: One
Two
One per port
One per open port
quiz.explanation: The IDS raises at most one alert per rule and source every 30 seconds, so the second scan inside that time adds no new alert, though it is still a full scan. This keeps a long scan from flooding the dashboard.

quiz.question: Which of these scans could stay below the CybICS port_scan rule? (Select all that apply)
options: One port every 5 seconds
An nmap ACK scan, with no SYN packets
A fast SYN scan of 1,000 ports on a single host
One port on each of many hosts
quiz.explanation: A slow scan never puts 5 ports in one window, an ACK scan sends no SYN packets, and a wide scan never reaches 5 ports per target. A fast SYN scan of many ports on one host is exactly what the rule catches.

quiz.question: Which MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique does the port_scan rule detect?
options: T0846.001 Port Scan
T0888 Remote System Information Discovery
T0842 Network Sniffing
T0830 Adversary-in-the-Middle
quiz.explanation: Scanning ports to find services is T0846.001, Remote System Discovery: Port Scan. T0888 is tempting because it also sounds like discovery, but it means reading a device's own information such as its firmware version; T0842 is passive listening, not knocking on ports.
